speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It should have been Elizabeth Barrack Browning and not Robert Barrack Browning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, it is not something that you immediately see or feel when you look out the window, unless you are outside in Ang Mo Kio on 13 May last year where Singapore's daily temperature hit 37°C for the first time in 40 years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will also not escape our attention that we have now gone from daily torrential downpours suddenly being replaced by the dry and hot weather.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And when I speak to older constituents, one thing that often comes up is how much more comfortable our climate seemed to be in the past; and the data backs it up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, my constituency of Sengkang is one in five regions listed as having very high urban heat vulnerability in Cooling Singapore's 2020 urban heat vulnerability analysis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I do not want to just focus on doom and gloom today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we can frame the problem we face in another way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we cannot, on our own, stop the climate from getting hotter, we can reduce the impact global warming has on the immediate environment around us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Reducing this impact is not just a matter of what is nice to do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to work to mitigate higher temperatures because, firstly, there are substantial social and economic costs if we do not do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we can do this because there are proven ways of doing so now and new ways in the future that I am optimistic we can develop with sufficient attention and investment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While spending of this scale is unlikely to be necessary for heat mitigation, mainly because many interventions can be made through regulation and private sector participation, I believe Singapore's strategies to mitigate and adapt to urban heat have to better take into account socio-economic issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also need to be accelerated and need to be given regulatory teeth.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I would like to point out some social economic dimensions to the urban heat problem that would help us identify principles and priority areas to work on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Last year, the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) and National Environment Authority (NEA) introduced a new Heat Stress Advisory for the public as well as introduce rules to reduce heat stress risks for outdoor workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are important developments in Singapore's workplace safety journey.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I believe the next step would be to tackle indirect but heat-related safety issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a well-studied phenomenon that humid heat exposure significantly increases thermal load during sleep and affect sleep quality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Alongside the adverse impact on mental health and other physical health effects that heat can cause, poor sleep quality paired with long work hours, are also known to contribute to a higher risk of workplace injury.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While dormitory standards for migrant workers were updated in 2021, there are many exemptions, including dormitories with leases expiring before 2034 and those with six beds of fewer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The new standards also introduced requirements for an adequate number of fans, but it appears that these requirements may be more COVID-19-related than heat-related as there are no temperature requirements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With many such dormitory residents operating heavy machinery or driving large vehicles, should we not be paying particular attention to sleep quality?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Research has also indicated that apart from having a greater impact on older people's sleep quality, heat also affects their mood disproportionately and other less thought about ways.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, some medicines for chronic diseases affect the body's ability to regulate body temperature.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment recently said in a supplementary question response that she would take up my suggestion to provide air conditioning at Residents' Committee venues and study rooms during prolonged and severe heat waves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that if and when implemented, this offering can be integrated into NEA's new Heat Stress Advisory so that residents who need this, particularly older people, are aware of this offering.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But perhaps the most obvious is the impact that urban heat has on those who are less well-off.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While better-off Singaporeans can simply turn on their air-conditioning or even afford to live in passively cool buildings, one of the few options available to the less well-off is to cool down with pool showers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Home Improvement Programme (HIP) and Climate-Friendly Households Programme could be good foundations for encouraging householders to take up heat- resilient efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, subsidies can be added for fans or blackout curtains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, could the existing Climate-Friendly Households Voucher Scheme be expanded beyond the 300,000, qualifying 1- to 3-room flats to support vulnerable residents living larger households?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Housing and Development Board (HDB) already designs HDB blocks and towns with wind flow and thermal comfort as considerations, it should also pay special attention to inequality and heat resilience when designing HDB blocks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Residents in rental flats and smaller flats should be prioritised in efforts to ensure thermal comfort and wind flow.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An interim solution could be to offer rental flat residents living in the warmest blocks of flats ready access to public air-condition venues in their immediate neighbourhoods during the hottest times of the day for much-needed respite.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, I understand that many old estates with rental flats were built when such high-quality modelling was not readily available.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Government develop quantifiable targets to retrofit old estates to deal with Singapore's heating?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The built environment industry transformation map has set some standards for future buildings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I suggest we apply some of these goals to older buildings instead of waiting for leases to run out.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is important to tackle these issues because the impact of urban heat on mental health, sleep quality, heat stress and physical health, for example, heat being a trigger factor for conditions, like asthma, on vulnerable groups is tangible and compounds other challenges they already face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But beyond what is necessary, vulnerable groups should also be accorded a decent living standard with regard to heat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Not only are these groups least able to adapt to climate change, they typically have contributed least to climate change causing carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second point I want to make is the importance of acting quickly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When I refer to tackling urban heat quickly, I do not mean disregarding or recklessly accelerating measures from research and development (R&D) to roll out.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What I mean is to carefully take into account pathway dependency or the constraints past decisions imposed on later decisions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sengkang Town Council will be closely following the results of the project, which is expected to conclude later this year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While many mitigation and adaptation concepts have only been tested in wealthier cities outside the tropics, some concepts should, theoretically, be feasible for trial in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Dutch city of Arnhem, for example, has aimed to reduce asphalt cover by 10%, as part of its climate change adaptation plan and has begun digging up asphalt in areas of low vehicular traffic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the Chinese city of Fuzhou, called a new furnace city for severe stress from the urban heat island effect brought about by urbanisation and climate change, a study of 31 urban parks found that they cool surrounding environmental land surface temperatures by an average of 2.9°C in summer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the precise impact of parks in Singapore are less well studied, Bishan Park can be up to about three degrees cooler than residential blocks in the city.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With many peripheral and non-core forests designated for development in the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA's) 2019 Master Plan and leaving aside the impact to biodiversity and carbon emissions, we should be doing our best to retain as many of these as possible – possibly in the form of parks because it takes decades and significant costs to re-establish such green spaces should authorities decide to reintroduce green spaces in the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, how does the latest URA Master Plan Review treat the retention of green cover?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does it give such considerations high or low priority?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are also social economic impacts with property prices near green spaces higher than those further away.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One study led by PhD student, Teo Hong Chen at the National University of Singapore's (NUS') Centre for Nature-based Climate Solutions found that in the 2010s, prices for a HDB flat rose by about $553 for every 1% increase of tree cover within 200 metres of the flat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Teo noted that with declining green areas across the country, buyers tend to value greenery near their homes a lot more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this contribution could be partly due to the perceived aesthetic and mental health benefits green spaces bring, what is evident is that such trends disadvantage those who can afford to spend less on their property.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps URA's plan, for every household to be within a 10-minute walk from a park by 2030, should take into account such considerations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the five regions listed as having very high urban heat vulnerability – in the urban heat vulnerability analysis – could be given additional attention, with green spaces retained and created around denser and lower income neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Since 2021, all new and existing public sector buildings undergoing major retrofitting, are required to attain super low energy certification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this is a substantial improvement from previous targets, the Government should accelerate plans to retrofit all public sector buildings in line with the super low certification as part of its commitment to having the public sector take the lead on sustainability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Particular focus should be placed on ensuring new buildings and building retrofits, near residential areas, meet super low energy certification in order to reduce heat emissions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Green Mark certification could also be updated to take into account the direct impact of buildings on their surroundings, in terms of heat, to incentivise shade and discourage excessive asphalt and concrete.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In some of these cases, there are intermediate solutions which could pave the way and ready the public for regulation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, ensuring that the National Stadium and other event venues do not prohibit visitors from bringing in their own water as a good start.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will go a long way in helping outdoor workers, such as delivery riders and construction workers as well as the general public, stay hydrated in a warming Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Every day, our environment gets hotter is a pivotal day for our country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not to say we should try and build a weather machine or an air-conditioned dome.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But what we are doing well, we should do as quickly as we can; and what we are doing wrongly or are planning to do wrongly, we should do differently – so that we are not locked into bad choices that our children will pay for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Rising temperatures will be compounded by the urban heat island (UHI) effect, as our densely built-up environment absorbs and retains heat; and activities, such as transportation and industrial works, generate heat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Various Members had previously filed questions on heat resilience, including just yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We would like to assure this House that the Government has, for some time now, and will continue to address this as part of our overall climate resilience efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, cooling strategies aim to keep us cool in our warm climate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Greening Singapore is a key strategy that has multiple benefits, including providing shade and reducing ambient temperatures of our surroundings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As we transform Singapore into a City in Nature, we are setting in place a network of green spaces across the island; and as the Member has said, by 2030, every household will be within a 10-minute walk from a park.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also intensifying greening, beyond just our parks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under our OneMillionTrees Movement, with the help of our partners and the community, we have planted over 630,000 trees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Other greening measures include increasing skyrise greenery and greenery on building facades, such as through the URA's Landscaping for Urban Spaces and High-Rises (LUSH) scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As part of greenery intensification efforts, under the Green Towns Programme, suitable top decks of HDB multi-storey car parks are converted to greenery and community or allotment gardens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also deploying other cooling strategies across the island.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Member may be aware, from the Ministry of National Development's Parliamentary Question response yesterday, that HDB conducts environmental modelling for new towns and estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This enables us to site new flats and orientate blocks to optimise wind flow and reduce heat gain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For existing towns, under HDB's Green Towns Programme, we are studying the application of cool coatings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides these broad-based measures, there are also specific measures to help various vulnerable groups cope with the impact of higher temperatures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, HDB has created more openings along corridors in some older rental blocks, by removing some units from each floor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This enhances airflow and natural ventilation in these blocks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Migrant worker dormitories are required to be provided with adequate fans to ensure good air circulation and ventilation in the dormitory rooms and recreation centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) is also installing ice machines in recreation centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The public can easily check the prevailing heat stress levels on the myENV app before, embarking on outdoor activities and take simple steps to protect ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is no different from checking the weather forecast for rain, in deciding whether to bring an umbrella.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Similar to the other weather data on the myENV app, readings shown are based on the monitoring station nearest to the app user automatically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We currently have nine WBGT stations island-wide and will be expanding our network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Access to water is important to address heat stress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have easy access to clean drinking water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singapore's tap water is perfectly safe for direct consumption, without the need for boiling or water filters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Furthermore, water dispensers are widely available at our hawker centres, parks, bus interchanges and terminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In fact, a Singapore University of Social Sciences undergraduate, Tng Ming Kang, has created a crowd-sourced map on these existing water dispensers in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also have targeted sector-specific guidelines for various groups, including outdoor workers, athletes, uniformed personnel, residential homes and schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MOM introduced an enhanced set of measures to reduce the risk of heat stress for outdoor workers last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These include measures focusing on four aspects: acclimatise, drink, rest and shade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Employers should also reschedule outdoor work to cooler parts of the day where feasible and re-deploy workers vulnerable to heat stress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Beyond MOM's guidelines, we are also heartened that organisations have taken additional steps to protect outdoor workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, Changi Airport Group provides refresh pods at staff rest areas, which circulate cool air at the touch of a button.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They also deploy trucks with isotonic drinks to remind workers to stay hydrated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And for our delivery workers, Grab and Foodpanda remind riders on heat stress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Deliveroo provides water for riders at its delivery-only kitchens and encourages merchants to do so too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, we set the Heat Stress Advisory thresholds in consultation with experts and we are reviewing our heat resilience plans, based on the climate projections from our Third National Climate Change study.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We leverage R&D to design more effective heat-resilience strategies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Researchers in NUS are also investigating the impact of warmer and more humid nights on sleep quality, to develop novel cooling solutions, such as smart systems that can adjust fan wind speed and air-con temperature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will ensure that rising temperatures do not take a toll on people's rest while we remain energy efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Cooling Singapore 2.0 project also investigates the impact of heat on different segments of the population, such as the elderly and children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We may also consider studying other relevant social-economic dimensions in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also cooperate with international partners on future collaborations and knowledge-sharing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Even as the Government takes steps to address warming temperatures and the urban heat island effect, I would like to call on the public to join us on this journey to make Singapore and our communities more heat-resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Individually, we can take steps to reduce heat emissions by taking public transport and using less air-conditioning and more energy-efficient electrical appliances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As a community, we can look out for one another and co-create solutions, such as setting up community cool spaces, to beat the heat together.
